Md Fazlul Karim with A Wahab, Saifuddin Ahmed, Fawzia Karim Feroze and Khandaker Aminul Haque, Advocates-For Plaintiff-Petitioner. 
Khandker Mahbub Uddin Ahmed with SM Munir, Advocates-For Defendants-Opposite Parties
parties:
Waliullah ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
Vs.
Hasina Begum & ors ----- Defendants- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
A.K. Badrul Huq, J: Seekers of Justice many a time are to take long circuitous routes both on account of hierarchy of Courts and Procedural law. Such seekers of Justice are and can be dragged to the last ladder of the said hierarchy and for receiving Justice they have to pass through a long arduous journey of procedural law. The present matter in hand can be depicted as one in this regard.

2. Redressal of grievance by granting restitution to defendants-opposite parties on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 laid under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code of Civil Procedure (for short The Code) by trial Court and sustained by Appellate Court in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 prompted plaintiff-petitioner to invoke this Court's Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115 of The Code on laying Revision Petition.

3. Portrayal of essential facts forming background of this Revision Petition as emerged from Revision Petition, Annexures annexed in Petition, Counter Affidavit filed by defendants-opposite parties, Judgments of Courts below which are under challenge in Revision Petition and paper and documents produced before this Court will be instructive in resolving controversy and those are succinctly stated hereunder:

a. Petitioner as Plaintiff on 5-9-1968 instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 in Third Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka for decree of eviction of licensee Defendants Md. Sekander Ali and his son Monu from properties described in Schedule A, B and C. Schedule A, B and C properties will be described hereinafter as suit property.

b. Suit was decreed ex parte on 27-2-1975. Immediate after, Decree was put to execution in Decree Execution Case No. 14 of 1975.

c. Defendant Md. Sekander Ali on 4-3-1975 filed a Petition under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code for setting aside Decree passed ex parte in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968. The Petition had been numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975.

d. Operation of ex parte decree was stayed by Court on 27-3-1975 on strength of a Petition laid by Defendant Md. Sekandar Ali in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975.

e. Petitioner in spite of order of stay dated 27-3-1975 on 23-8-1980 evicted Defendant Md. Sekander Ali from suit property. The eviction matter was brought to notice of Court and Court by order dated 30-8-1980 directed petitioner to hand over possession to Defendant Md. Sekander Ali within 24 hours.

f. Appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 400 of 1980 filed by Petitioner against said order dated 30-8-1980 stood dismissed by Appellate Court by Judgment dated 29-9-1980.

g. Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code was carried by Petitioner against the Appellate Judgment. Civil Revision Petition had been numbered as Civil Revision No. 1321 of 1980. Rule issued on Civil Revision Petition was made absolute by High Court Division by Judgment dated 26-2-1991 and Appellate Judgment was set aside. High Court Division recorded direction to dispose of Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 within one (1) month of receipt of record since said Miscellaneous Case was pending for 15 years.

h. Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code was allowed by Judgment dated 9-9-1991 and ex parte Decree dated 27-2-1975 recorded in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 was set aside.

i. Defendant Md. Sekander Ali on 28-10-1991 submitted a petition under section 144 read with section 151 of The Code for restitution of possession on suit property. The Petition had been numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991. Miscellaneous Case was rejected on 19-11-1992 on ground that Petitioner of Miscellaneous case in support of his claim did not produce any document nor did prove his claim in accordance with law.

j. Review Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code, thereafter, had been presented on 2-1-1993. Petition was numbered as Review Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995.

k. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Dhaka by Judgment dated 9-7-1997 allowed Review Miscellaneous Case and recorded order for restitution of possession suit property. In recording restitution on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case learned Senior Assistant Judge considered respective case of parties, perused and examined record, pleadings of parties and rendered decision that Petition laid under section 144 of The Code and record of Decree Execution Case No. 14 of 1975 were placed and tagged with the record of the case and since ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code and since suit was restored to its file and number, Petitioner of Miscellaneous Case (Md. Sekander Ali) was entitled to restitution of possession on suit property and predecessor Court through oversight rejected Petition laid under section 144 and section 151 of The Code and by that justice had been impaired seriously. In rendering decision learned Senior Assistant Judge took into account Judgment and orders passed in different proceedings between parties which went upto High Court Division. Learned Senior Assistant Judge, also, took into account Basaratullah being dead his heirs Fazle Karim and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 1996 BLD (AD) 9. Learned Senior Assistant Judge directed Opposite Party of Review Miscellaneous Case and Petitioner of this Revision Petition to hand over possession on suit property to petitioner, here Opposite Partyside in Revision Petition by way of restitution.

l. Petitioner felt aggrieved of above adjudication and sought setting aside through a Medium of appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 before learned District Judge, Dhaka. Learned District Judge, Dhaka by Judgment dated 24-7-2002 dismissed appeal and maintained decisions rendered by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka with partial modification. In dismissing appeal learned District Judge considered submissions brought home from both sides, examined record and Judgment under challenge in appeal and, also, took into account authorities such as Hamejuddin Howlader and another vs Mainuddin Shaikh and another, 10 DLR 645, Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar, 34 DLR (AD) 209, Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others, 36 DLR 1 and Keramat Ali Bhuiyan being dead his heirs Shahida Khanom and another vs Ramizuddin Ahmed Bhuiyan, 43 DLR (AD) 58. Learned Appellate Judge recorded following decisions:

(i) Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code was allowed and ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 was set aside and suit was restored to its file and number and all relevant papers and documents had been in record and court which passed order under Review did not take into consideration all those matters and on strength of section 144 of The Code Petitioner of Miscellaneous Case (Present Opposite Partyside) got entitlement to get possession by way of restitution. Learned Appellate Judge, also, rendered decision that Court committed wrong in rejecting Petition for restitution on 19-11-1992 and by that justice had been seriously jeopardised.

(ii) Opposite Party (present Petitioner) of Miscellaneous Case illegally dispossessed Md. Sekander Ali from his lawful possession and Sekander Ali was entitled to get restitution in accordance with law and learned Senior Assistant Judge correctly passed order dated 9-7-1997.

(iii) Review Miscellaneous Case was not barred by limitation. Learned Appellate Judge modified partially order of learned Senior Assistant Judge dated 9-7-1997 in the terms that Petitioner to Miscellaneous Case (present Opposite Partyside) would get restitution through Court.

4. Feeling still dissatisfied, Petitioner approached this Court in this Revision Petition.

5. Md. Sekander Ali having been dead, his heirs, sons, daughters and wife have been substituted in proceedings and heirs are Opposite Party Nos. 1-8 in this Revision Petition.

6. Statements contained in Revision Petition have been controverted from side of Opposite Parties on Presentation of a Counter Affidavit. Statements made in Counter Affidavit are that Defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 under Order IX, rule 13 of The Code for setting aside ex parte decree dated 27-2-1975 passed in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 and an application for stay of all further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1973 was filed in said Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1973 and Court allowed application and stayed all further proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1975 by its order dated 27-3-1975. But Petitioner suppressing the said order of stay managed to evict Defendant side from properties of A, B and C schedule of plaint on 23-8-1980. Executing Court detected fraud practised upon Court by Petitioner and directed petitioner to hand over possession on properties described in A, B and C schedule of plaint within 24 hours by its order dated 30-8-1980. All those orders were in record but when judgment dated 19-11-1992 was passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991 Petitioner separated those orders from record and, as such, Court found that opposite parties did not file those orders and rejected said Miscellaneous Case and, thus, application for Review was allowed when those orders were located in record.

7. Mr Md. Fazlul Karim along with Mr A Wahab, Mr Saifuddin Ahmed, Ms Fawzia Karim Firoze and Mr Khandaker Aminul Haque, learned Counsels appeared for Petitioner. Opposite Parties are represented by Mr Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr SM Munir, learned Counsels.

8. Sustainability of decisions recorded by courts below has been assailed raising five Branches of contentions and those contentions have been repelled from side of Opposite Parties.

9. First Branch of contention pressed into service is in respect of scope of section 144 of The Code. Restitution can be sought by any party entitled to any benefit by way of restitution before Court of first instance when a decree is varied or reversed and unless a decree is varied or reversed, question of restitution does not arise since decree had not been varied or reversed by superior Court, it is contended. In support of contention reliance has been put on U Maung Gyee vs U Ba Tin, AIR 1928 Rangoon 293, Gopal Paroi vs Swarna Bewa, AIR 1931 Calcutta 14, Kundan Kishanlal vs Board of Revenue Uttar Pradesh at Allahabad and others, AIR 1972 Allahabad 184, Ashutosh Nandi and another vs Kunda Kamini Dasi and others, 33 CWN 908 and Industrial Electric Corporation Ltd vs Kalimuddin Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 951.

10. Contentions so raised have been repelled from side of Opposite Parties in putting forward rival contentions that setting aside and reversal got similar meaning and even if section 144 of The Code is not attracted, restitution can be very much made in invoking inherent jurisdiction of Court under section 151 of The Code.

11. Rival contentions advanced from both sides may now be addressed.

12. The word "Restitution" has not been defined in The Code. The word "Restitution" stated in Wharton's Law Lexicon, Fourteenth Edition is hereunder:

"The restoring anything unjustly taken from another; also putting in possession of lands or tenements who had been unlawfully disseised of them."

13. In Black's Law Dictionary, Sixth Edition, Restitution has been stated thus:

"An equitable remedy under which a person is restored to his or her original position prior to loss or injury, or placed in the position he or she would have been, had the breach not occurred, Act of restoring; restoration; restoration of anything to its rightful owner; the act of making good or giving equivalent for any loss, damage or injury; and indemnification."

14. In Corpus Juris Secundum (CJS) 77 Restitution is defined in the following terms:

"as meaning the act of restoring; restoration; restoration of anything to its rightful owner; act of making good, or of giving an equivalent for any loss, damage, or injury; indemnification; the action of restoring or giving back something to its proper owner; that of making restoration to one for loss or injury previously inflicted

At common law the word "restitution" was employed to denote the return or restoration of a specific thing or condition, but in modern usage restitution may go beyond the act of returning the thing taken, and in its broad sense, is not confined to the return of something of which one has been deprived, but includes compensation for loss, damage, or injury done to another.

15. In Halsbury's Laws of England law of restitution has been couched in the following language:

Where a wrongful or irregular execution has been set aside or where a judgment or order has been reversed after execution thereon has taken place, restitution will be made to the successful party. The order setting aside the execution or reversing the judgment or order should provide for this; and if it does execution may issue upon it in the ordinary course. If the order does not so provide, another order may be made, or a writ called a writ of restitution be issued commanding the judgment-creditor to restore the property or pay over the proceeds of sale.

<u>16. Restitution is, thus, restoration of anything to a person from which it was taken away earlier, return of something of which one has been deprived, act of making good for loss, damage and injury.</u>

17. Section 144 of The Code postulates that where and insofar as a decree is varied or reversed, the Court of first instance shall, on the application of any party entitled to any benefit by way of restitution or otherwise, cause such restitution to be made as will, so far as may be, place the parties in the position which they would have occupied but for such decree or such part thereof as has been varied or reversed; and, for this purpose, the Court may make any orders, including orders for the refund of costs and for the payment of interest, damages, compensation and mesne profits, which are properly consequential on such variation or reversal.

18. The principle of restitution is that on the variance or reversal or setting aside of a judgment, order or decree when the person deprived of right to any property through an erroneous judgment he may be entitled to restitution of his right or property and that it is the duty and obligation of a Court to do justice to seekers of justice.

19. The judicial Committee of Privy Council while examining the question under section 144 of The Code in Jai Berham vs Kedar Nath Marwari, AIR 1922 (PC) 269=LR 491A 351 observed:

It is the duty of the Court to place parties in the position which they would have occupied but for the wrong decree.

The Judicial Committee then observed:

The duty of the Court to grant restitutk n arises even outside the provisions of section 144.

The Judicial Committee further observed:

"Nor indeed does this duty arise merely under the said section and it is inherent in the general jurisdiction of the Court to act rightly and fairly according to the circumstances towards all the parties involved."

20. The Supreme Court of India in Lal Bhagwant Singh vs Sri Kishen Das, AIR 1953 SC 136 in dealing on Doctrine of Restitution observed:

The Doctrine of restitution is that on the reversal of a judgment the law raises an obligation on the party to the record, who received the benefit of the erroneous judgment, to make restitution to the other party for what he had lost and it is the duty of the Court to enforce that obligation unless it is shown that restitution would be clearly contrary to the interests of justice.

21. Our Appellate Division, also, dealt with the scope and applicability of section 144 of The Code in Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar, 34 DLR (AD) 208. Appellate Division in the said case considered good number of authorities on section 144 as well as section 151 of The Code. Appellate Division, also, considered the decision of The Judicial Committee of Privy Council in Jai Berham vs Kader Nath Marwari (Supra). The observation of The Appellate Division is couched in following language:

'Restitution' simply means restoration of something to a person from which it was taken away earlier under an erroneous judgment of a court. Question of restitution arises when the erroneous judgment of the court is varied, reversed or set aside. Section 144 of The Code which provides for restitution says that restitution thereunder is available when a decree is varied or reversed.

22. Restitution, if not covered under section 144 of The Code, can be, also, made in exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code. Section 151 of The Code does not formulate any new doctrine but only gives a legislation recognition of the well known doctrine and principle that every court has inherent power to act ex debitio justitiae and to do that real Justice for the administration of which alone it exists. It is always to be remembered that under inherent power court acts ex debitio justitiae according to equity, justice and good conscience of a cause and in consonance with fundamental principles of Judicial procedure. Justice is the pursuit and end of all law. Justice is divine and all procedure and technicality must bend to the cause of justice.

23. The Calcutta High Court in Birendra Nath Basu Thakur and another vs Surendra Kumar Basu Thakur and others, 44 CWN 438 considered the power of Court to direct restitution in inherent Jurisdiction under section 151 of The Code. Calcutta High Court relying on the Privy Council case of Jai Berham vs Keder Nath Marwari (Supra) held:

The power of a court to direct restitution is inherent in the Court itself. It rests on the principle that a court of justice is under a duty to repair the injury done to a party by its acts.

24. In Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar (Supra) our Appellate Division, took into account various authorities of Indian Jurisdiction and held:

Section 144 is not exhaustive and it only defines the procedure for restitution in the case of a reversal of a decree. In the case of reversal of an order the same remedy should be given by the court in the exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of The Code. The inherent power of the Court should be exercised at its discretion, according to the merit of the case. This discretionary power cannot be exercised when restoration, if allowed, will run counter to the interest of justice.

In the case restitution was sought under section 144 of The Code and Appellate Division treated the said Petition under section 144 of The Code to be one under section 151 of The Code to meet the ends of justice.

25. In the interest of justice in the case of variance, reversal or setting aside an order /judgment/decree restitution can be very much made under inherent power as envisaged in section 151 of The Code. To put it differently, in the case of setting aside, variance and reversal of judgment remedy of restitution, if cannot be granted under section 144 of The Code, should be given by court in the exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code.

26. I shall now address myself to authorities relied upon from side of Petitioner. Before adverting to authorities it is to be kept in view that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be made applicable to particular fact and generality of expression that may be found cannot be regarded as proposition of whole law but must be regarded as governed and qualified by particular facts of case in which such expression occurs. It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or a sentence from the Judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration and treat it to be complete law. Keeping in view this proposition of law authorities cited may now be approached and considered.

27. In U Mating Gyee vs U Ba Tin, AIR 1928 Rangoon 293, Principle enunciated is that section 144 of The Code gives no discretion to learned Judge and restitution should be ordered as a matter of course in order to bring about status-quo ante.

28. In Gopal Paroi vs Swarna Bewa, AIR 1931 Calcutta 14, Principle propounded is that section 144 of The Code only applies where a decree is "varied or reversed" and it is perfectly certain that a decree is only varied or reversed by a superior Court on appeal or on revision or it may be, on reference and if a decree is set aside either by a proceeding in suit itself or if it is set aside by a decree in another suit altogether or if, without being set aside by such a decree, is superseded those are matters which are not within the words of section 144.

29. In Kundan Kishanlal vs Board of Revenue, Uttar Pradesh at Allahabad and others, AIR 1972 Allahabad 184 principle settled is that where an ex parte decree is set aside, it cannot be said that decree has been varied or reversed. A decree can be varied or reversed on appeal or in some similar proceedings. When an ex parte decree is set aside, a new decree is passed, thereafter, and that decree cannot be said to be result of any variation or reversal of any prior decree. It is further stated that a restitution in such a case may be claimed under section 151 of The Code. In the case it is, also, settled that a decree can be varied or reversed in exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code.

30. In Ashutosh Nandi and another vs Kundal Kamini Dasi and others, 33 CWN 908 principle emerged is that provision in section 144 of The Code that Court which is to make restitution is Court of firs instance implies a Court decree of which is reversed by a Court of Appeal and section 144 only refers to cases where a decree of Court of first instance is reversed on appeal or revision.

31. In Industrial Electric Corporation Ltd vs Kalimuddin Ahmed and others, 21 DLR 951 principle that has been enunciated is that principle of restitution whether based on section 144 or section 151 of The Code is that when a Judgment is reversed, the law raises an obligation on the party who received benefit on erroneous judgment to make good to other party that very thug which he had obtained from him. Under such circumstances it is duty of Court to enforce that obligation unless it is shown that that would be contrary to real justice of case. It has been further stated that there are circumstances where restitution can be granted which is not strictly covered by provision of section 144 of The Code of Civil Procedure in exercise of inherent powers of Court. Lal Bhagwant Singh vs Sri Kishen Das AIR 1953 SC 136 had been referred to and relied upon in the case.

<u>32. From above authorities, principles emerged is that restitution can be sought and made when a decree obtained by a Decree-Holder stands varied, reversed and set aside and restitution can be very much granted on strength of section 144 of The Code and, also, on strength of inherent power envisaged under section 151 of The Code. I am in complete agreement with principles enunciated in above authorities. But I am afraid that petitioner cannot derive any benefit from the aforesaid authorities.</u>

<u>33. In case in hand ex parte decree recorded on 27-2-1975 in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1975 laid by defendant Md. Sekander Ali. Decree passed since stood set aside, possession of parties was required to be placed to that position before ex parte decree that is to bring about status-quo ante Md. Sekander Ali on presentation of petition under sections 144 and 151 of The Code sought restitution of possession on suit property. Learned Trial Judge on a consideration of proceedings between parties, different orders, fact and circumstances of case recorded order of restitution on allowing Review Miscellaneous Case and said decision recorded by learned Senior Assistant Judge was maintained by Appellate Judge canvassing reasons. No exception can be taken to the decisions rendered and conclusion reached by the Judges.</u>

34. Second Branch of contention brought home from side of Petitioner is that Review Miscellaneous Case was barred by limitation in as much as order under review was dated 19-11-1992 and Review Miscellaneous Case was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 and case stood barred on the face of record.

35. Countering the said contention it has been contended from side of Opposite Parties that Review Miscellaneous Case had been filed on 2-1-1993 and that was very much within time fixed by law and not barred by limitation.

<u>36. Annexure-C to Revision Petition is Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 read with section 151 of The Code. On careful scrutiny it appears that Petition was filed on 2-1-1993 but it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995. It is not known what was reason for registering Miscellaneous Case in the year 1995. Mere registration of case in year 1995 cannot make Opposite Parties out of Court on point of limitation when Petition under Order XLVII, rule 1 and section 151 of The Code had been presented on 2-1-1993 within period of limitation fixed by law which is 90 days as provided in Article 173 of The Limitation Act.</u>

37. Third Branch of contention pressed is on Jurisdiction of Judge to review order under Review Miscellaneous Case. It has been emphatically submitted from side of Petitioner that Judge who passed order under review was not the same Judge who reviewed order. Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code and Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others 36 DLR 1 had been referred to in support of contention.

38. Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code is quoted hereunder:

"2. An application for review of a decree or order of a Court, not being High Court Division, upon some ground other than the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, shall be made only to the judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed; but any such application may, if the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 4, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), be disposed of by his successor."

39. Reading of Order XLVII, rule 2 of The Code demonstrates that if ground for review is discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on face of decree, then review will lie to Judge who passed decree or made order as well as to his successor in office. But if review is made on any other ground then it shall be made only to Judge who passed decree or order sought to be reviewed. It is, thus, grounds which are material for forum of presentation of Review Petition. The above view adopted has been, also, expressed in Paragraph No. 24 in Judgment delivered in Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others, 36 DLR 1 on which reliance has been put and great emphasis has been given from side of Petitioner, though, the same is of no assistance to Petitioner. Paragraph No. 24 is quoted hereunder:

"24. Rule 2 however has qualified the application of rule 1 as far as the ground and forum for review are concerned. If the ground for review is the discovery of such new and important matter or evidence as is referred to in rule 1 or the existence of a clerical or arithmetical mistake or error apparent on the face of the decree, then the review will lie to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order as well as to his successor in office. Review on these grounds are entertainable and disposable by the Court which passed the decree or made the order. The presence or absence of the original Judge who passed the decree or made the order is immaterial. But if an application for review of a decree or order is made on any other ground, then rule 2 provides that the said application "shall be made only to the Judge who passed the decree or made the order sought to be reviewed." So, it is the ground of review which makes all the differences in the forum for review. If, however, the Judge who passed the decree or made the order has ordered notice to issue under rule 1, sub-rule (2), proviso (a), the application for review may be disposed of by his successor."

40. Under Order XLVII, rule 1 of The Code a review can be made when there is error apparent on the face of the record.

<u>41. Review was sought canvassing ground that all papers were kept in record and order passed by Court directing restitution of suit property within 24 hours had been, also, in record and Court through oversight did not take into stock of above and there had been error apparent on face of record. Omission to advert to apply mind to papers already on record and failure to take into consideration those papers is an error which is very much apparent on face of record. Rule 2 of Order XLVII of The Code is not at all attracted in case of Opposite Parties. May be Petition had not been articulated properly but bad pleading cannot oust a litigant public seeking justice from Court. It is always to be kept in view that it is the substance and not the form which is to be looked at and considered. Moreover, Review Petition had been presented to Judge who passed order under Review and Judge having been transferred, successor Judge disposed of Review matter. There was, as such, no want of Jurisdiction on part of learned Senior Assistant Judge in disposing of Review Miscellaneous Case. Proposition of law propounded in Alhaj Md. Ruhul Amin vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and others (Supra).</u>

42. Bar of Order XLVII, rule 8 of The Code in disposal of restitution matter along with Review Miscellaneous Case has been Fourth Branch of contention. Contention has been pressed that Review matter was required to be disposed of after making note in Register but Court at once heard original case ie restitution matter. Gour Krishna Sarkar and another vs Nilmadhab Saha and others, AIR 1923 Calcutta 113 has been relied upon on the above contention.

43. Repelling said contention it is contended from side of Opposite Parties that Order XLVII, rule 8 of The Code is no bar in hearing original matter ie restitution matter, while disposing Review matter.

<u>44. Review is allowed on reviewing Judgment/Order or Decree under review. Order passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge was sought to be reviewed and only point that survived for determination before Reviewing Court was whether the order dated 19-11-1992 rejecting Miscellaneous Case No. 69 of 1991 laid under sections 144 and 151 of The Code demanded review or not and that matter could be decided and disposed of in disposing of Review Miscellaneous Case. Rules, procedures and technicalities of law cannot stand in the way in administration of justice and seekers of Justice cannot be denied justice on the plea of breach of rules, procedural hurdles and technicalities. It is well settled that principal object behind all legal formalities is to safeguard paramount interest of justice and mere technicalities unless offering an insurmountable hurdle should not be allowed to defeat the ends of justice. No insurmountable hurdle transpired in deciding the restitution matter in disposing Review Miscellaneous Case. Authority placed got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case and, as such, I do not like to make an idle parade of discussing the same.</u>

45. Fifth and Last Branch of contention advanced from side of Petitioner is that Decree of eviction had been passed only in respect of property of Schedule-C to plaint and not in respect of properties of Schedule-A and B but Opposite Parties sought restitution in respect of properties of all the three schedules ie Schedule A, B and C and restitution, thus, cannot be granted in respect of properties of Schedule A and B.

46. Said contention has been countered from side of Opposite, Parties pressing into service contention that Writ of Delivery of possession was in respect of Schedule-A, B and C properties and Petitioner got possession over Schedule-A, B and C properties and decree had been varied, reversed and set aside in respect of Schedule-A, B and C properties and, as such, Opposite Parties are entitled to restitution in respect of Schedule-A, B and C -properties. Challenge has been thrown by Opposite Parties to Petitioner to substantiate the plea on producing copy of Writ of Delivery of possession and copy of Execution Case showing that decree was put into execution only in respect of Schedule-C property and not in respect of Schedule A and B properties and Petitioner got possession only of 'C' schedule property.

47. In order to get myself satisfied from which property Opposite Parties were evicted and Petitioner got possession and what schedule property had been stated in Decree Execution Case. I wanted papers from the Petitioner side but those papers could not be produced before me.

48. In Revision Petition plaint of Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 has been annexed as Annexure-A. On examination of the Plaint it transpires that there are three (3) schedules, Schedule A, B and C and decree of eviction had been sought in properties described in Schedule 'A' 'B' and 'C' and there is no such averment that though Schedule-A and B had been given, actually eviction was sought only in respect of Schedule-C property. Reliefs sought are hereunder:

"a) a decree for eviction of the defendants in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants;

b) delivery of vacant possession of the suit land and the suit but therein to the plaintiff after removing all obstacles and obstructions of the defendants there from;

c) all costs of the suit;

d) other ancillary relief or reliefs which the plaintiff is legally or equitably entitled to."

49. From certified copy of judgment of ex parte decree which has been produced before me from side of Petitioner it appears that decree was in respect of whole properties of Three Schedules. The ordering portion is quoted hereunder:

"Order

that the suit be decreed ex preterit cost.

The defendant be evicted from the suit premises after removing all obstructions there from.

<u>50. The judgment itself manifests that the Decree of eviction was in respect of suit premises and suit premises comprises of Schedule-A, B and C properties and Defendant Md. Sekander Ali, the predecessor of present Opposite Party Nos. 1-8 stood evicted from suit premises in execution of decree and since the decree recorded in Title Suit No. 261 of 1968 stood set aside, reversed and varied in respect of properties described in Schedule-A, B and C, Opposite Parties who are legal heirs of Md. Sekander Ali are entitled to have restitution of possession in respect of A, B and C schedule properties.</u>

51. All Five Branches of contentions pressed into service from the side of Petitioner could not impress me and those having been devoid of any substance stand ruled out.

52. Examination of decision, reason and conclusion reached by learned Senior Assistant Judge and maintained by learned Appellate Judge with modification it does not indicate that those suffer from any illegality, legal infirmity, perversity and error of law. The decisions rendered and reason assigned in leading to decision and conclusion reached appear to have been informed by tradition and methodised by analogy.

53. In exercising Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of The Code two conditions are to be satisfied:

i. There must be an error of law resulting in an error in the decision and

ii. By that error a failure of justice has been occasioned.

Mere error of law is not the only ground for interference in Revisional Jurisdiction under section 115 of The Code and along with error of law it is to be demonstrated that a failure of justice has been occasioned by that error of law and only then interference by this Court can be called for, otherwise not. It has already been posited that decisions rendered and conclusion reached by Courts below neither appear to have suffered from error of law nor a failure of justice seem to have been occasioned.

54. The inevitable conclusion that flows is that rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code is without any merit and the same, thus, fails. Rule stands discharged.

55. Order staying operation of the Judgment/Order dated 24-7-2002 recorded by learned District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 177 of 1997 affirming Judgment and order dated 9-7-1997 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 1995 stand vacated.

56. Regard being had to fact and circumstances of the case I direct the parties to bear their respective cost.

Copy of this Judgment be transmitted to courts below.
